introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, ONE from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde imprime « Answer FOUR questions, ONE from each section. All questions carry equal marks », mais le sujet ne comporte AUCUNE section imprimée (six questions numérotées 1 à 6, sans titre de section). `regles_choix` = parmi 4 sur 6 avec `groupes` = ["PAPER 2"] dans tous les fichiers ; la mention « une question par section » est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown` et ne peut pas être appliquée faute de sections.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées d'après les notions classiques du programme de Géologie A Level, sans source consultable. Les valeurs chiffrées sont des ordres de grandeur de cours (formulation « about »). Les faits à faire relire par un géologue avant mise en avant sont signalés ci-dessous.

Le sujet ne comporte aucune figure imprimée : `figures` est vide dans tous les fichiers. Les schémas utiles (« value of clear sketches ») sont décrits dans les corrigés (éléments à dessiner, légende) sans valeurs inventées.
Points : 8 + 12 + 5 = 25, conformes au sujet. Dans le fichier, (b) regroupe (i), (ii) et (iii) = 12 points imprimés pour l'ensemble.

Question 2(a) : « trigonal » est traité comme système à part (comme le sujet le propose) ; le corrigé précise que certains manuels le rattachent au système hexagonal (division rhomboédrique). Le sujet ne dit pas combien de différences sont attendues : le corrigé en donne huit, une par point du barème.

Question 2(b) : les valeurs de dureté (6,5 à 7), de densité (3,2 à 4,4) et les paramètres de maille sont des valeurs classiques de cours, formulées avec « about » ; la répartition des 12 points entre (i), (ii) et (iii) n'est pas imprimée, le corrigé traite les trois parties à égalité.

Question 2(c) : le sujet demande d'« esquisser » (outline) les processus de différenciation d'un magma basaltique primaire ; le corrigé en donne six (cristallisation fractionnée, tri par gravité, filtre-presse, assimilation, mélange de magmas, immiscibilité) ; 5 points imprimés.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) In a tabular form, give the essential differences between the tetragonal and trigonal crystal systems.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **tetragonal** system has three axes at right angles, two equal and one different, with one four-fold axis of symmetry; the **trigonal** system (treated here as a separate system, although many books class it as the rhombohedral division of the hexagonal system) is referred to four axes, three equal horizontal axes at $120^\circ$ and a vertical axis, with one three-fold axis of symmetry. The essential differences are:

| Feature | Tetragonal system | Trigonal system |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Number of crystallographic axes** | Three axes: $a_1$, $a_2$ and $c$ | Four axes (Miller-Bravais): $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ and $c$ (or three equal rhombohedral axes) |
| **2. Axial lengths** | $a=b\neq c$ (two equal horizontal axes, a different vertical axis) | $a_1=a_2=a_3\neq c$ (rhombohedral axes: $a=b=c$) |
| **3. Angles between the axes** | All angles are $90^\circ$ ($\alpha=\beta=\gamma=90^\circ$) | The three horizontal axes are $120^\circ$ apart and $c$ is $90^\circ$ to them (rhombohedral axes: $\alpha=\beta=\gamma\neq 90^\circ$) |
| **4. Principal axis of symmetry** | One **four-fold** axis (the $c$ axis) | One **three-fold** axis (the $c$ axis) |
| **5. Cross-section perpendicular to $c$** | Square (or eight-sided) | Triangular, or six-sided (hexagonal) |
| **6. Characteristic forms** | Tetragonal prisms, tetragonal bipyramids, trapezohedra, pyramids | Trigonal prisms, **rhombohedra**, scalenohedra, trigonal pyramids and trapezohedra |
| **7. Number of symmetry classes** | Seven | Five |
| **8. Examples** | Zircon, rutile, cassiterite, chalcopyrite, vesuvianite | **Quartz**, calcite, dolomite, haematite, corundum, tourmaline |

**Sketches to draw:** the axes of each system (three axes at right angles with one longer or shorter $c$ axis for the tetragonal; the three horizontal axes at $120^\circ$ plus $c$ for the trigonal) and a typical crystal of each: a short tetragonal prism capped by a bipyramid (zircon) and a rhombohedron (calcite) or a prism with rhombohedral terminations (quartz).

The **olivine group** is a group of **ferromagnesian silicate minerals** that are the commonest minerals of the upper mantle and of ultramafic and basic igneous rocks (dunite, peridotite, gabbro, basalt).

**(i) Structure and composition.**

- Olivine is a **nesosilicate (island silicate)**: the structure is built of **independent (isolated) $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedra** that are not linked to each other by shared oxygens. The tetrahedra are bonded together by the positive ions (**$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$**), each surrounded by six oxygens in octahedral co-ordination. Because the structure is compact and the bonds are strong in all directions, the mineral is hard and has no good cleavage.
- General formula: **$(\mathrm{Mg,Fe})_2\mathrm{SiO_4}$**. The two end members form a **complete solid solution series** because $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ have similar ionic radii and the same charge and can replace each other: **forsterite $\mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4}$** (magnesium-rich, high melting point, about 1890 °C) and **fayalite $\mathrm{Fe_2SiO_4}$** (iron-rich, lower melting point, about 1200 °C). Common olivine in rocks is rich in forsterite (about $\mathrm{Fo_{80}}$ to $\mathrm{Fo_{90}}$). Other members of the group are tephroite ($\mathrm{Mn_2SiO_4}$) and monticellite ($\mathrm{CaMgSiO_4}$).
- Olivine is silica-poor (no quartz is found in equilibrium with it) and is the **first mineral to crystallise** in the discontinuous branch of **Bowen's reaction series**; at lower temperature it reacts with the melt to form pyroxene.

**(ii) Crystallography.**

- Olivine crystallises in the **orthorhombic system** (three unequal axes at right angles, $a\neq b\neq c$, $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=90^\circ$; class $mmm$, dipyramidal).
- Well-formed crystals are **rare**; they are short prismatic or tabular, with prism and pinacoid faces. Olivine is most often found as **small rounded grains (granular masses)** in igneous rocks, or as phenocrysts in basalt.
- It is often replaced along cracks by **serpentine** (alteration to green-black serpentine, "serpentinisation") in the presence of water.

**(iii) Diagnostic physical properties.**

| Property | Olivine |
|---|---|
| Colour | **Olive-green** to yellow-green (forsterite, colourless to pale green); fayalite is brown to black |
| Lustre | **Vitreous (glassy)** |
| Hardness (Mohs) | About **6.5 to 7**, scratches glass |
| Cleavage | **Poor or indistinct** (not diagnostic) |
| Fracture | **Conchoidal** (like glass) |
| Specific gravity | About **3.2 (forsterite) to 4.4 (fayalite)**, increasing with iron |
| Streak | White (or colourless) |
| Transparency | Transparent to translucent; the gem variety is **peridot** |
| Other | Occurs in rocks that have **no free quartz**; weathers readily to reddish iron oxide and serpentine |

Thus olivine is identified in hand specimen by its **green colour, glassy lustre, granular habit, high hardness, conchoidal fracture and lack of cleavage**, and by its occurrence in basic and ultrabasic rocks.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Outline the differentiation processes that occur in a primary basaltic magma.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **primary basaltic magma** is formed by the partial melting of the upper mantle (peridotite). **Magmatic differentiation** is the group of processes by which this single parent magma gives rise to a **variety of igneous rocks** of different composition. The main processes are:

1. **Fractional crystallisation (Bowen's reaction series).** As the magma cools, minerals crystallise in a definite order, the **high-temperature, silica-poor minerals first** (olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase, then pyroxene, amphibole, biotite and sodium-rich plagioclase). When the early crystals are **separated** from the liquid, the remaining melt becomes progressively richer in **silica, sodium, potassium and water**, so that it changes from basaltic to andesitic, then to rhyolitic (granitic) composition.
2. **Gravity settling (crystal settling) and floating.** The dense early crystals (olivine, pyroxene, chromite) **sink** to the floor of the magma chamber and form **cumulates** (layered ultramafic and gabbroic rocks, as in layered intrusions); light crystals may float.
3. **Filter pressing and flow differentiation.** The residual liquid is **squeezed out** from the crystal mush by earth movements (filter pressing), and crystals are concentrated in the centre of a dyke or sill by the flow of the magma (flow differentiation).
4. **Assimilation (contamination).** The magma **melts and absorbs country rock** (xenoliths), or reacts with it, so that its composition changes (for example, richer in silica).
5. **Magma mixing.** Two magmas of different composition (basaltic and granitic or andesitic) **mix** to give an intermediate magma.
6. **Liquid immiscibility.** The magma separates into **two liquids that do not mix**, as oil and water, one rich in silica and one in iron-magnesium (or sulphide), which form different rocks.

Among these, **fractional crystallisation** is the most important process, and it explains how a single basaltic magma can produce the series from gabbro to granite.
